sections.h2: When does unpaid property tax lead to a sale in New Mexico?
sections.html:
The state can sell a house at public auction once its taxes have been delinquent for three years. Section 7-38-65 NMSA 1978 says real property may be sold for delinquent taxes at any time after three years from the first date shown on the tax delinquency list on which the taxes became delinquent. The sale must be offered within four years of that date, with an extension if a court or other legal bar prevents it.

The debt starts earlier than the sale. Under 7-38-48, taxes on real property are a lien against the property from January 1 of the tax year, and the lien is a first lien that outranks every other interest, perfected or not. The lien continues until the taxes, penalty and interest are paid.

Interest runs on its own clock. Section 7-38-49 says that if taxes are not paid within thirty days after they are due, interest accrues from the thirtieth day at one percent a month or any fraction of a month. Interest is not charged on interest or on any penalty.

A 2013 amendment, effective January 1, 2014, requires the department to offer at least one property from each county's delinquency list for sale every year, unless the department director and the county treasurer agree in writing to postpone.

sections.h2: Does New Mexico sell tax liens or the property itself?
sections.html:
The sources reviewed for this page describe a sale of the real property itself, followed by a deed. The Taxation and Revenue Department's Property Tax Division sells delinquent real property at public auction under 7-38-65, usually at the county courthouse or a similar location the department designates in the county where the property sits. The sources do not describe a sale of tax lien certificates to investors.

County treasurers have a separate tool for mobile homes. The department's auction page explains that under 7-38-53 the county treasurer may seize a mobile home and sell it for taxes under a demand warrant.

The department does not hold sales in all 33 counties every year. Its page says there is no fixed schedule, and sales are scheduled as title research is completed and other collection efforts are exhausted. When the page was last updated, it listed a San Miguel County auction on November 19, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. Check the current list at the department's auction page or call the Property Tax Division at (505) 827-0883.

sections.h2: How does the auction work, step by step?
sections.html:
The auction follows requirements in 7-38-67 and the department's published terms. The main points:

  • Notice: published in a local newspaper at least once a week for the three weeks before the week of the sale, stating the time, place and a property description.
  • Location: held in the county where the property is located, by the department or a hired auctioneer.
  • Minimum price: not less than the total of delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs. The department must also consider the value of the owner's interest when setting it.
  • Registration: bidders register on the day of sale. The department's FAQ says registration begins at 8 a.m. and closes at 10 a.m. when the auction starts.
  • Bidding: oral, in person or through an agent with a notarized authorization.
  • Payment: in full by the close of the auction, by cashier's check, money order, or a personal or company check backed by a bank letter of guarantee.

If a property does not sell, it may be offered later, but the notice requirements apply again to each sale. The department may re-offer a property for less than the minimum bid if it did not sell for at least that amount.

sections.h2: How can an owner stop the sale?
sections.html:
By paying everything owed, or signing an installment agreement, by 5:00 p.m. on the day before the sale. Section 7-38-65 lists both options: all delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs paid by that deadline, or a written installment agreement under 7-38-68 entered by then.

The installment agreement has limits worth knowing:

  • It cannot run more than thirty-six months.
  • Interest accrues on the unpaid balance at one percent a month.
  • Signing it is an irrevocable admission of liability for the taxes covered.
  • As long as the terms are met, it prevents further collection action on those taxes.
  • The division may proceed with collection if payments are missed, other property taxes go unpaid, or another condition is broken.
  • After a breach, the original delinquency date is used for timing a sale, and the division will not enter another agreement for the same taxes.
  • The division cannot enter an agreement on or after the date of the initial sale.

sections.h2: What rights does a former owner have after the sale?
sections.html:
New Mexico does not give former owners a right of redemption, but they have two years to challenge the sale in court. The department's FAQ states that the state has no right of redemption for former owners. It describes the two-year period under 7-38-70 as the window in which the former owner, or someone claiming through them, can bring a court challenge. The only redemption period the department mentions is the 120-day federal IRS redemption period, which applies if the federal government holds a lien on the property.

Section 7-38-70 sets out what a challenger must prove to defeat the buyer's title. Any one of the following is enough:

  • The property was not subject to taxation for the tax years in question.
  • The division failed to mail the required notice or to receive any required return receipt.
  • The challenger had title at the time of sale and had paid all delinquent amounts before it.
  • The challenger had an installment agreement and made every payment on time.

Annotations show that courts also look at notice. One case found notice constitutionally inadequate when it went only to an old address after the owner had filed a change of address with the assessor. A 2024 Court of Appeals decision, Dearborn v. Clarke, held that the department can invalidate a tax sale that was not conducted in substantial compliance with the tax code, so long as no deed has been issued. In that case the sole bidder paid the minimum price of $17,100.

sections.h2: What does the buyer receive, and what stays on the property?
sections.html:
The buyer receives a tax deed that works like a quitclaim and carries no warranty. The department says the deed conveys all of the former owner's interest as of the date the state's lien arose, subject only to perfected interests existing before that date. It adds that the sale extinguishes the tax lien only. No other liens are extinguished, and the buyer must inspect the property and review the chain of title before bidding.

Sales are as-is, final and without refunds, and the buyer indemnifies the department for environmental conditions, according to the department's terms. Buyers cannot trespass while inspecting.

sections.h2: Is it better to sell before the auction?
sections.html:
For an owner with equity, selling first is often worth checking, because the minimum bid is set by the debt rather than by the home's value. Section 7-38-67 sets the minimum price at the taxes, penalties, interest and costs owed. A bidder can win at that number if nobody offers more. An annotation to 7-38-67 describes the department's duty to recognize the owner's interest in any amount above the debt, but the owner is not in control of how high bidding goes.

A private sale that closes before the deadline gives the owner control of the price and the timing. The title company can pay the delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs from the proceeds at closing, which satisfies the condition in 7-38-65 if it is done by 5:00 p.m. the day before the auction. The sale needs a buyer who can close quickly and accept the house in its present condition.

Cash Home Buyers buys New Mexico houses as-is and does not promise a price in advance. If your home is on a delinquency list or you have received a sale notice, tell any buyer the auction date at the start, because the closing has to be scheduled around it. A tax attorney or the Property Tax Division can confirm the payoff figure.

faqs.q: How long before New Mexico can sell my house for back taxes?
faqs.a: At least three years after the first date the taxes appear on the delinquency list. Under 7-38-65 the property must then be offered within four years of that date, unless a legal bar delays it.

faqs.q: Does New Mexico have a redemption period after a tax sale?
faqs.a: No, the Taxation and Revenue Department says the state has no right of redemption for former owners. The only redemption period it mentions is the 120-day federal IRS period. Former owners have two years to challenge the sale in court under 7-38-70.

faqs.q: Does a tax sale wipe out my mortgage?
faqs.a: The department says the sale extinguishes the tax lien only and no other liens. The deed is subject to perfected interests that existed before the property tax lien arose. Ask an attorney how that applies to your loan.

faqs.q: Can I make payments instead of losing the house?
faqs.a: Yes, through an installment agreement under 7-38-68, if signed by 5:00 p.m. the day before the sale. It runs up to thirty-six months at one percent monthly interest, and the division cannot enter one on or after the initial sale date.

faqs.q: How much interest accrues on unpaid New Mexico property tax?
faqs.a: One percent a month or any fraction of a month, starting on the thirtieth day after the tax is due, under 7-38-49. No interest is charged on interest or on any penalty.

faqs.q: Where are New Mexico tax auctions held?
faqs.a: Usually at the county courthouse or a similar location the department designates in the county where the property sits. The department does not hold sales in all 33 counties each year.
